prize_parts.citation: For introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into the theory of international trade, and for showing how reallocation across firms shapes the gains from trade.

statement.case_for: B001 pairs a clear conceptual advance with unusually broad empirical uptake. Melitz (2003) and Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple (2004) moved trade analysis from representative-firm and industry-level models to firms that differ in productivity and select into exporting or FDI. That created a new account of the gains from trade through reallocation and gave empirical researchers a framework for firm-level microdata. It asks a big question, why some firms export and what that does to welfare, and has influenced many researchers beyond trade. This matches the standard I described in 2023, where a model and the data it organises together make the contribution. The core papers are more than twenty years old and have been tested in many countries. The credit is concentrated in two names, which keeps the citation tight.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. The empirical facts about exporter premia (Bernard, Jensen) and the parallel Eaton-Kortum line sit outside the credited names, so a Helpman-Melitz award could look like it under-credits the wider firm-level trade programme. Redding's quantitative and spatial work is also left out. Some detailed predictions of the baseline model are rejected, and welfare conclusions depend on distributional assumptions, so part of the lasting value lies in the extensions and not in the original model.

responses.point: Hassler ranks the BLP demand-estimation and dynamic-oligopoly work (B006) first. He argues it has high methodological and applied impact beyond IO, is fully mature after decades of use, and that the core BLP credit is clean for Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes.
responses.response: I agree the BLP core is cleanly attributable and thoroughly mature, and it is why I rank B006 third and list it as an alternative. My hesitation is the boundary of the discovery. B006 bundles demand estimation, dynamic games and production-function strands, and the three-name limit forces Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin out. B001 has a single sharply identifiable conceptual break, from representative to heterogeneous firms, that changed what researchers model and what they measure. I would not dismiss the tool-building case, but I judge the Helpman-Melitz boundary to be more defensible.

responses.point: Stromberg places B006 first and B001 second. He argues that BLP reshaped empirical IO and is used in antitrust, trade and health. He also notes that B001's credit is concentrated in Melitz and Helpman, and that Redding's work is more derivative.
responses.response: We agree on the attribution of B001, including leaving Redding out of a minimal award. I would not use how long a field has gone without a prize as an argument for either candidate, since that is not evidence of scientific merit. Where I differ is on the unit of discovery. A prize for B006 would reward a set of estimation methods whose identification rests on strong functional-form assumptions, as Teorell notes. B001 supplies both a framework and an explanation of observed firm behaviour. I would want the committee to compare them on that basis.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B030 second. He notes that any three-person selection must choose between the technology and tasks strand (Autor, Katz) and the trade-shock strand (Hanson, Dorn). He also flags overlap with recent prizes and continuing debate over how persistent the trade-shock effects are.
responses.response: That is the main reason I keep B030 as an alternative rather than my first choice, even though I ranked it second and it is close to my own field. The work combines a conceptual framework with credible quasi-experimental evidence on a major societal question. Even so, the attribution is not clean. The task framework has originators outside the credited names, and the Autor-Dorn-Hanson trade-shock papers and the Autor-Katz skills literature are two partly separate bodies of work. The Goldin-Katz skill-demand work also overlaps with the 2023 prize. I would need a convincing way to draw a single discovery boundary before preferring B030 to B001.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B001 first. He accepts Melitz and Helpman as the core but warns that Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are important parallel contributors outside the credited set, and that this limits a clean two-person attribution.
responses.response: I agree this is the largest risk, and it is why I list it as my main uncertainty. Two points limit it. Melitz (2003) is the model that introduced selection into exporting with heterogeneous firms, and Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple give the export-versus-FDI sorting result. Eaton-Kortum is a different, Ricardian framework, and Bernard-Jensen's empirical facts motivated rather than replaced the theory. I am working only with the credited list, so I cannot add those names, and I would not stretch the citation to cover them. The citation should be worded so that it does not overclaim the whole field.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum as co-originators who should affect how narrowly the citation is drawn. They are not credited on this ballot entry.
Whether Redding's quantitative and spatial work belongs in the core credit or is better seen as a later extension. I treat it as an extension.
How much weight to give detailed rejections of the baseline model's predictions, and the sensitivity of its welfare results to distributional assumptions, relative to its influence on practice.
For the B030 alternative, whether the task-based framework and the China-shock evidence form one discovery or two, and how persistent the trade-shock effects are.
For the B006 alternative, whether demand estimation and dynamic oligopoly models should be treated as one discovery or two, and whether to prefer a methodological contribution over a substantive one.
I have not independently verified citation counts, priority claims or award history. My assessment rests on general knowledge and the supplied openings.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My listed frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler) are not credited on any shortlisted ballot entry. B030 is close to my own field of labour economics, and I presented the 2023 prize to Goldin, but I see no personal or collaborative connection to its credited names.
